title: Microbial contamination of keyboards and electronic equipment of ICU (Intensive Care Units) in Kashan University of medical sciences and health service hospitals
author: Nazeri, Salmani Arani, et al.

steps.title: Select and record equipment
steps.instruction: Randomly select 75 computer keyboards and bedside electronic equipment from the five ICUs during routine daily activity and record for each item the location, type, number of users (medical or non‑medical staff), disinfection method, and disinfectant used.

steps.title: Sample surfaces with saline swab
steps.instruction: Using a sterile swab moistened with normal saline (and an alcohol lamp if needed), roll the swab over the most frequently used keys (Enter, Space bar, P, D, K) covering an area of approximately 16 cm²; similarly sample the touch keys of other equipment over an equivalent 16 cm² area.

steps.title: Transfer swabs to broth
steps.instruction: Place each swab into a test tube containing Tryptic Soy Broth, seal, and transport to the laboratory as quickly as possible.

steps.title: Plate and incubate samples
steps.instruction: Streak each broth‑enriched swab onto Blood agar and MacConkey agar plates (Himedia, India) and incubate the plates at 37 °C for at least 48 hours.

steps.title: Identify bacterial isolates
steps.instruction: Examine growth colonies and perform conventional identification: gram stain, colony morphology, colour, hemolysis; for Gram‑positive isolates conduct catalase, coagulase, novobiocin sensitivity, and bile‑esculin tests; for Gram‑negative isolates perform oxidase and IMVIC tests to differentiate Enterobacteriaceae.

steps.title: Statistical analysis
steps.instruction: Enter all identification data into SPSS version 16 and analyze using chi‑square tests.

description: Nowadays, health care infections and the associated high mortality rate is very high in many hospitals [1]. Nosocomial infections are one of the most important infections, that occur in patients hospitalized due to non-infectious diseases and are considered as one of the main causes of mortality in hospitals, which subsequently increase the cost of health cares for the health system [[2], [3], [4], [5], [6]]. Recently, nosocomial infections are considered as the most important causes of mortality and morbidity among patients admitted in to Intensive Care Unit (ICU) while the majority of patients admitted in to these wards are immunocompromised. In addition, the bacterial agents of this diseases are multidrug-resistant (MDR) that could cause many problems for health care facilities and enormous challenges for physician and hospital administrators around the world [[7], [8], [9], [10], [11]]. The worldwide prevalence of nosocomial infections are estimated near 10% while in Iran it has been reported between 1.3–10% [[12], [13], [14], [15], [16], [17]]. Only in the United States, more than two million nosocomial infections were reported which cost more than 4.5$ million and has resulted in 90,000 deaths annually [18]. Medical staffs and nurses are supposed to be a common mode of exogenous transmission through their hands. The role of the hospital environment as a reservoir of nosocomial pathogens has been controversial [19]. However, electronic equipment and computers at the bedside of patients in health service hospitals can contribute to the transmission of pathogens in hospital infections [20,21]. In different studies, keyboards are known as the reservoirs of pathogens, because they are used at the rooms where the patients are especially because of repeated contacts with the hands of the personnel [1,19,22].
